title: The Good and Goods of a Christian Liberal Arts Education
author: Elizabeth Stice
summary: Elizabeth Stice, who teaches in a Great Books honors program at a Christian liberal arts university, uses the start of the semester to ask what such an education is for. Her guide is Josef Pieper, whose distinction between the world of work, where things matter for some further purpose, and activities meaningful in themselves frames her defense of the curriculum. Every author on the reading list, from Aeschylus to Arendt and Hildegard to Hobbes, is presented as an attempt to touch the core of reality, and the program's goal, following Pieper's essay on learning how to see again, is to restore students' spiritual capacity to perceive reality as it truly is. Stice extends the argument beyond honors to the general humanities sequence, to extracurriculars such as choir, ceramics and memorizing poetry, and to a faculty chosen for its care about deeper things and about students. The essay's critical turn is institutional: as struggling Christian colleges close or retreat into professional programs, they submit to a world defined by work and fail to capitalize on the K-12 classical renewal. She insists graduates are employable, but argues the real case for Christian liberal arts rests on contemplation and preparation for more than the workplace.
points: Stice adopts Pieper's test of activity meaningful in itself as the criterion for what belongs in a Great Books curriculum: works that seek, even remotely, the core of all things.
Following Pieper's warning that the human ability to see is in decline, she defines the program's aim as teaching students to perceive visible reality as it truly is.
Contemplation is not confined to reading lists; poetry memorization, music, run club and ceramics are presented as further forms of reaching toward the foundation of reality.
She warns that financially stressed Christian colleges treat the liberal arts as ballast and pivot to professional programs, having almost lost faith in what they do best.
She notes the missed opportunity of rising K-12 classical education, arguing students arrive wanting to understand their existence, not only their employment prospects.
quotes: For advocates, these books are not only good, but somewhat easily identifiable. It is obvious to some people why our program should be like the title of Nadya Williams’s book and podcast: Christians Reading Classics. But for skeptics or the uninitiated, it may be unclear which books count and why.

The books and authors we assign all encourage contemplation and reflect attempts to touch “even remotely, the core of all things.” They may not all clearly apprehend the “hidden ultimate reason of the living universe, the divine foundation of all that is,” but they are seeking it. You can see it from Aeschylus to Arendt, from Hildegard to Hobbes.
Pieper is not worried about whether or not students need glasses, he is concerned about “the spiritual capacity to perceive the visible reality as it truly is.

At a Christian liberal arts school, or in a Great Books program, we want our students to be employable. But we don’t want to just teach them things to transition smoothly into the working world. We want to help them transition into a way of being in reality that rests on the divine foundation of all that is.

Last year several students in our program memorized Seamus Heaney’s poem “The Rainstick” after Malcolm Guite visited and charmed us all with it. We also have students involved in run club, or who sing in school choirs, or who study ceramics. Reaching out in contemplation is more than one type of reading or assignment or extracurricular activity.

The liberal arts are in decline almost everywhere, but they may be especially vulnerable within Christian higher education, because so many smaller Christian colleges and universities are closing. And, in many cases, the liberal arts are treated as ballast by universities in trouble.

And while across the country, K-12 classical education is on the rise, Christian colleges are not fully capitalizing on the opportunity presented. It is almost as though we have lost faith in what it is we do best.

They are interested in employment, but they are also interested in the nature of their existence and their relationship to things beyond the workplace. Exclusively vocational curriculum or exclusively secular pedagogy do not deliver these goods.
